newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - EU court tax ruling will dent UK finances.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU court tax ruling will dent UK finances.

text.p: The European Court of Justice ruled on Thursday that two companies have paid too much value-added tax (VAT) to the British government, a decision which may cost the government millions of pounds.

The ruling, based on European Union law which aims to harmonise tax regulations across the continent, opens the floodgates to many similar claims and is another headache for the government as it prepares the November 26 budget.

The European Court upheld that toiletries manufacturer Elida Gibbs, a subsidiary of Anglo-Dutch giant Unilever, and retail chain Argos paid too much VAT on goods sold to customers under special discount offers.
In such cases VAT was payable on the discounted and not the full price, the decision said.
According to court documents, Unilever asked the British government to repay 884,000 pounds ($1.4 million). Argos asked for 1.4 million pounds.
The British Treasury said the total cost of cases such as these would run to about 200 million pounds.

"At the most extreme the loss would be around 200 million pounds in back tax, and back tax will only be payable if traders can substantiate claims going back 23 years," the Treasury said in a statement.

And if draft legislation seeking to limit the scope of VAT refunds is successfully completed, the cost could be much lower still, the Treasury said. "We think costs will be around 70 million pounds under the three-year limit rule."
The legislation, due to be introduced along with the budget, proposes a three year limit on refund claims.
But leading tax experts said Customs & Excise, which made the calculations, may be underestimating the problem.
"I think they are playing down the figures," said Alan Buckett, VAT partner at Binder Hamlyn and President of the National VAT Practitioners Council.

"The 200 million pound estimate sounds about right if the Treasury is treating the three-year limit draft legislation as if it were law already. Without it, costs could run as high as 500 million sterling," he said.
Companies are already planning to challange the ruling under European law, he said.
Thursday's ruling settles one of several big cases the government is fighting on VAT collection.
One of the biggest claims so far has been brought by a host of companies challenging legislation which prevents them claiming VAT on fleet vehicles.
And another case which could dent public finances concerns VAT on interest-free credit deals.
Earlier this year, the Court of Appeal upheld a claim by furniture company Primback which argued it had overpaid VAT when selling goods on interest-free credit.
